note:
ISO 2026-W29 runs from July 13 through July 19. Mars is about 0.2° in ecliptic longitude from Aldebaran in Taurus. To find Venus, first identify Leo, trace the Sickle, and locate Regulus in that pattern. Venus lies about 3.8° away in ecliptic longitude at the Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot; use the finder to transfer from Regulus to the planet.

**Naked eye:** 🌑 New Moon — 09:43:37 UTC. The dark Moon favors faint targets and extended star fields. Use Antares, Kornephoros, Atria, Larawag as the week’s fixed-sky framework.

**Planets:** Moon: Naked eye; magnitude -6.1; direct motion; 3.1% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Solar conjunction in ecliptic longitude Jul 14 09:43 UTC. Conjunction with Mercury in ecliptic longitude Jul 14 06:26 UTC. Conjunction with Venus in ecliptic longitude Jul 17 15:05 UTC. Conjunction with Jupiter in ecliptic longitude Jul 15 03:49 UTC. Mercury: In solar glare; magnitude 5.6; retrograde motion; 0.9% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Solar conjunction in ecliptic longitude Jul 13 01:25 UTC. Conjunction with Moon in ecliptic longitude Jul 14 06:26 UTC. Venus: Naked eye; magnitude -4.1; direct motion; 64.3% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Conjunction with Moon in ecliptic longitude Jul 17 15:05 UTC. Mars: Naked eye; magnitude 1.3; direct motion; 94.5% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Ceres: Telescope; magnitude 9.0; direct motion; 99.0% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Jupiter: In solar glare; magnitude -1.8; direct motion; 100.0% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Conjunction with Moon in ecliptic longitude Jul 15 03:49 UTC. Saturn: Naked eye; magnitude 0.7; direct motion; 99.7% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Uranus: Binoculars; magnitude 5.8; direct motion; 100.0% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Neptune: Telescope; magnitude 7.7; retrograde motion; 100.0% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Pluto: Substantial telescope; magnitude 14.5; retrograde motion; 100.0% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot.

**Binoculars:** Trace the charted figure of Aps, then identify β Aps at its plotted position.

**Small telescope:** M107: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; NGC 6193: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; Great Hercules Globular: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; Turtle Nebula: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; M12: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; NGC 6231: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance

story_candidates.dek: Antares is a star in Sco of catalogue visual magnitude 1.06; its declination determines which latitudes can observe it.
story_candidates.body:
The stored catalogue gives a visual magnitude of 1.06. This is a catalogue value, not a prediction of its brightness this week. Lower magnitudes mean brighter objects; sky brightness and altitude affect whether you can see the star.

Its catalogue position is approximately right ascension 16h 29m and declination -26.4°. These reference coordinates describe its sky location; they are not an observing time or a current altitude.

At the almanac’s default latitude of 45° N, this star rises and sets, reaching approximately 19° altitude at upper culmination. These are geometric calculations from declination, excluding refraction and local obstructions. Darkness and the time of culmination must still be checked for the observing date and your location.

How to find it: Establish the preserved Sco constellation figure from its labeled reference stars, then use the target’s plotted position rather than searching for an isolated star.

Sources: Star Almanack’s stored fixed-object and expanded Bayer catalogues; accepted constellation figures and guiding-star routes. Visibility limits are original geometric calculations from catalogue declination, not weekly predictions.

Why it is here: The Calendar selected Fixed object 332 as one of this week’s fixed-sky observing targets.

How to find it: Establish the preserved Sco constellation figure from its labeled reference stars, then use the target’s plotted position rather than searching for an isolated star.
